HOME ABOUT CONTACT Search articles ← Back to Home TECH · EVERYDAY SCIENCE Why Does Your Battery Look "Pregnant"? 😭 The Weird Science Behind Battery Swelling By Sakshi Madgundi · 2026 Okay, let's talk about something you've probably seen at least once but may never have wondered about. You pick up your old phone or open your laptop and suddenly notice that something looks... off . The back of the phone is bulging. The trackpad of the laptop looks slightly raised. Or the battery itself looks like someone put a tiny balloon inside the device. 😭 And that's when people usually say: "Bro... the battery is pregnant." 😭 Funny name. Not-so-funny reason. That swelling can actually tell us something interesting about what's happening inside the battery. First: What Kind of Battery Are We Talking About? Most modern phones, laptops, tablets and many other portable electronic devices use lithium-ion batteries . These batteries work through electrochemical reactions. During charging and discharging, lithium ions move between different parts of the battery. So yes, there is some pretty serious chemistry happening inside that tiny battery sitting in your phone. 😭 And that chemistry is also part of the reason battery swelling can happen. So... Is There Actually Gas Inside? This is the weird part. A lithium-ion battery is a sealed cell. Under normal conditions, it is designed to operate without visibly expanding. But when unwanted chemical reactions occur inside the cell, they can produce gases . Those reactions can become more likely as a battery ages or if it experiences things such as excessive heat, physical damage, electrical stress or other abnormal conditions. Because the battery cell is sealed, the gas can increase the pressure inside it. And eventually... the battery can start to swell. The battery isn't filling up with ordinary air. Gases can be produced by chemical reactions happening inside the battery cell. Wait... So Did the Electricity Turn Into Gas? 😭 Nope. This is probably the easiest thing to misunderstand. Electricity doesn't simply enter the battery and magically turn into gas. A lithium-ion battery stores energy through electrochemical processes . If the chemistry inside the cell becomes unstable or unwanted side reactions occur, those reactions can generate gases. So the swollen battery is more like a sign that something has gone wrong with the chemistry inside the cell . That's why the word lithium-ion actually matters when we're talking about this phenomenon. But What About Overcharging? Now we get to the part that you've probably heard everywhere: "Don't overcharge your battery!" And there is some truth behind that. Overcharging or other forms of electrical stress can damage lithium-ion cells and can contribute to unwanted chemical reactions. But here's the important part: Overcharging is not the only reason a battery can swell. Battery swelling can also be associated with aging, repeated use, excessive heat, physical damage, manufacturing problems and other abnormal conditions. So leaving your phone plugged in once doesn't mean you're going to wake up the next morning to a "pregnant phone." 😭 Why Does the Battery Actually Bulge? Think of the battery as a tightly packed little system. Inside are different materials, including electrodes, a separator and an electrolyte, all arranged so that the battery can store and release energy. When gases are generated inside the sealed cell, pressure can build up. Some lithium-ion batteries use flexible packaging, especially pouch-type cells. That packaging can expand when the internal pressure increases. And that's the moment when your perfectly normal device suddenly starts looking like: "I have gained 5 kg overnight." 😭 Is a Swollen Battery Dangerous? This is where the joke should stop. A visibly swollen battery should not be treated as normal. A damaged lithium-ion battery can become a safety concern because, under certain conditions, a cell can heat up uncontrollably. This phenomenon is called thermal runaway . In severe cases, thermal runaway can lead to venting, smoke, fire and other hazardous battery failure. So that funny little bump on the back of your phone isn't something to simply ignore. What Should You Do If You Notice It? If a phone, laptop or another device has a visibly swollen battery, don't try to push it back into place. And please don't poke it. Don't puncture it, crush it, open it or try to "release the gas." A damaged lithium-ion cell can be hazardous, so the safer approach is to stop using the affected device and have it inspected by the manufacturer, an authorised service centre or a suitably qualified technician. If the device becomes extremely hot, starts smoking, leaks or shows other serious signs of failure, move away from it and seek appropriate professional or emergency assistance. And What About Charging? One simple habit is to use the charger and cable appropriate for your device and avoid exposing the device to unnecessary extreme heat, especially while charging. Also pay attention to unusual behaviour. If your battery suddenly becomes very hot, starts swelling, drains unusually quickly or behaves very differently from before, don't just assume: "Eh, it's probably fine." 😭 Batteries don't usually swell for no reason. The Simple Science Behind the "Pregnant Battery" So let's put everything together. Your phone or laptop probably uses a lithium-ion battery . Inside that battery, electrochemical reactions allow it to store and release energy. As the battery ages or experiences abnormal conditions, unwanted chemical reactions can occur. Those reactions can generate gases. The gas increases pressure inside the sealed cell. And that pressure can make the battery bulge or swell . So no, electricity didn't turn into gas. 😭 The swelling can happen because chemical reactions inside a lithium-ion battery generate gas and increase internal pressure. So... Is the Battery Actually "Pregnant"? 😭 Obviously... No. 😂 But the nickname makes the phenomenon surprisingly easy to remember. That strange bulge is basically your battery's way of saying: "Something inside me isn't going as it should." And now you know that there's actually some fascinating chemistry behind that weird-looking bump. A tiny battery may look simple from the outside. Inside? It's chemistry doing a lot more than we usually realise. A Note on Sources This article is a simple, friendly explanation of lithium-ion battery swelling. The technical points were checked against battery-safety information from UL Research Institutes and manufacturer guidance from Samsung . Battery behaviour can vary depending on the device, battery chemistry, design and condition. This article is intended for general information and is not a repair guide. © 2026 Beyond The Obvious · Sakshi Madgundi

HOME ABOUT CONTACT Search articles THE GODS WHO WERE FORGOTTEN 🔥 Before Yellamma: Who Was Renuka Really? The Story Behind the Goddess By Sakshi Madgundi · 2026 There is a name that appears in temples, village traditions, Puranic stories and devotional songs across parts of India: Renuka. Today, she is worshipped in different forms and under different names — Renuka Devi, Yellamma, Renukamba, and others. In the familiar Sanskritic story, she is remembered primarily as the wife of the sage Jamadagni and the mother of Parashurama, the warrior-sage regarded as an avatar of Vishnu. But there is a question hiding underneath that familiar story: Was Renuka always simply “the mother of Parashurama”? The answer is more complicated than the usual story suggests. And that is where her story becomes much more interesting. The Renuka We Usually Hear About The best-known story places Renuka in the household of the sage Jamadagni. She is described as exceptionally devoted and powerful through her ascetic discipline. In one famous episode, her spiritual power is associated with her ability to perform an extraordinary daily task: carrying water in an unbaked clay pot. Then one day, something changes. Renuka sees a group of celestial beings bathing in the river. Her concentration falters. The unbaked pot can no longer hold together. When she returns home, Jamadagni becomes furious. He commands his sons to kill their mother. Several refuse. Parashurama obeys. Jamadagni, pleased with his son's obedience, grants him a boon. Parashurama asks that his mother be brought back to life. Renuka is restored. The basic episode appears in Sanskrit literary traditions including the Mahabharata and later Puranic literature, although the details vary between versions. But something important is easy to miss. In these early narrative contexts, Renuka is not necessarily the central character. The story is largely being told as part of the larger story of Parashurama . Renuka is his mother. Jamadagni is his father. The episode explains something about Parashurama's character, obedience and extraordinary place within the tradition. But later, Renuka begins to become something much larger. The Woman Behind the Mother When we move beyond the familiar Parashurama story, Renuka starts appearing in a much wider religious landscape. She is worshipped in parts of Maharashtra, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Tamil Nadu , sometimes under names or forms connected with local mother-goddess traditions. Renuka and Yellamma became closely associated in several South Indian traditions. And this is where we have to be careful. It would be tempting to say: “Renuka was originally an ancient goddess, and later Hindu texts simply turned her into Parashurama's mother.” But there isn't enough evidence to state that as an established historical fact. Instead, what we can see is something more fascinating: multiple traditions appear to have converged around the figure of Renuka. One academic study describes the development of Renuka's mother-goddess identity as a complex process involving the merging of different personalities and myths. In other words, the Renuka worshipped in a village shrine does not necessarily have to be understood through only one Sanskrit story. Her identity grew through text, oral tradition, regional worship and local goddess traditions. From Renuka to Yellamma One of the most important transformations happens in Karnataka and neighbouring regions. Renuka becomes associated with Yellamma . Yellamma is not simply a different spelling of Renuka. The traditions surrounding her developed within particular regional and social contexts, and there are multiple versions of her story. Researchers studying Yellamma specifically note that versions of her legend differ from region to region. That means there isn't one universally fixed “Yellamma story.” Instead, there are many Renukas . There is the Renuka of Sanskrit epic and Puranic literature. There is the Renuka of regional temple traditions. There is Yellamma of northern Karnataka. There are traditions identifying her with other local mother goddesses. And there is the Renuka worshipped at important shrines such as Mahur in Maharashtra. The boundaries between these traditions are not always neat. And perhaps that is the point. Was Renuka Originally a Goddess? This is where things become controversial. Some modern writers and researchers have proposed that the Renuka/Yellamma tradition absorbed or was connected with older local mother-goddess traditions . One study argues that the later Renuka-Yellamma tradition may represent a process in which local goddess traditions became connected with the Sanskritic story of Renuka and Parashurama. But claims such as “Renuka was definitely a pre-Vedic goddess” or “Renuka was definitely a historical queen” go beyond what the evidence can securely establish. There are later regional accounts that portray Renuka in very different ways — including traditions that give her royal or local origins. One modern study examining these traditions, for example, discusses accounts connecting her with the Vidarbha region and with a possible queenly identity. These are regional/traditional interpretations, not established historical biography . And that distinction matters. Because the mystery isn't solved by replacing one legend with another. Then What Happened to Her? Perhaps the most remarkable part of Renuka's story is what happens after her death and resurrection . In later traditions, the episode becomes connected with ideas about Renuka's transformation into a goddess. Some versions contain an extraordinary detail: because Parashurama was in haste while restoring his mother, the head and body were mistakenly joined incorrectly. This becomes one explanation for unusual forms of Renuka/Yellamma worship in some regional traditions. The story therefore stops being merely: “Parashurama's mother was killed and brought back.” It becomes: “A woman who crossed death became a goddess whose identity could transcend the boundaries of caste, family and ordinary human life.” Different communities interpreted this transformation differently. And over time, Renuka's name became attached to traditions that were much broader than the original Parashurama narrative. The Goddess With Many Names Across different regions, Renuka/Yellamma is associated with several names and forms. She may appear as: Renuka Yellamma Renukamba Ekvira Yamai and other regional forms of the mother goddess. This doesn't necessarily mean that all these goddesses began as exactly the same deity. Rather, it shows how Indian religious traditions have historically allowed local and wider traditions to overlap . A village goddess could become identified with a figure known from Sanskrit literature. A Sanskrit figure could acquire new stories in a regional tradition. A mother goddess could be given a new genealogy. And a story could travel from text into song, temple ritual and oral tradition. Renuka is a remarkable example of that process. So… Who Was Renuka Before Yellamma? The honest answer is: We don't have enough evidence to give her one definitive “original identity.” What we can establish is that the Renuka known from Sanskrit traditions became connected over time with much broader regional goddess traditions. In the Mahabharata and Puranic narratives, she is prominently remembered as Jamadagni's wife and Parashurama's mother . In later regional traditions, she becomes a powerful mother goddess in her own right. And in Yellamma traditions, she takes on an identity that cannot be reduced to simply being Parashurama's mother. That transformation is perhaps more interesting than a simple origin story. Because Renuka's story isn't only about who she was . It is about how a figure changes when a story travels across centuries, regions and communities. The Renuka We Remember Today, when someone says “Renuka,” they might be thinking about Parashurama. Someone else might think of Renuka Devi at Mahur. Someone in Karnataka might think of Yellamma. Someone else may know her through a local village goddess tradition. All of them are looking at the same name through different layers of tradition. And perhaps this is why Renuka belongs in a series called: The Gods Who Were Forgotten Because maybe Renuka was never really forgotten. Perhaps we simply forgot that she had more than one story. A Note on Sources The story of Renuka and Parashurama occurs in multiple Sanskrit traditions, including the Mahabharata and Puranic literature, while the identification of Renuka with Yellamma and other regional goddesses belongs to later and regional religious traditions. These traditions contain variations, so this article distinguishes between textual narratives, regional traditions and modern scholarly interpretations rather than presenting one version as the single historical truth. © 2026 Beyond The Obvious · Sakshi Madgundi

excerpt: There is a strange story hidden inside one of the oldest surviving collections of Indian sacred poetry.

HOME ABOUT CONTACT ANCIENT STORIES · INDIAN MYTHOLOGY Mārtāṇḍa: The Forgotten Eighth Son of Aditi By Sakshi Madgundi · 2026 There is a strange story hidden inside one of the oldest surviving collections of Indian sacred poetry. It begins with Aditi . She had eight sons. Seven of them went with her to the gods. But the eighth? She cast him away. His name was Mārtāṇḍa . And what makes his story even stranger is what happens next. Aditi eventually brought him back — for birth and for death. So who exactly was Mārtāṇḍa? Was he an ancient form of the Sun? Was he connected with the origin of mortal beings? Or was he something even older that later traditions came to understand differently? The Rigveda never gives us a simple answer. The Story Begins With Aditi Today, Aditi is widely remembered as a divine mother and the mother of the Ādityas . But the oldest Vedic material does not always present mythology in the neat genealogies familiar from later Hindu traditions. One of the most mysterious passages appears in Rigveda 10.72 , a hymn concerned with the generations and emergence of the gods. The hymn says that Aditi had eight sons born from her body. But she went to the gods with only seven. The eighth was Mārtāṇḍa. And he was cast away. Why? The hymn doesn't tell us. There is no dramatic explanation. No battle. No punishment. No story about something Mārtāṇḍa had done wrong. Just a remarkably strange statement: Aditi had eight sons — and rejected one. That one was Mārtāṇḍa. The Name Mārtāṇḍa Is Strange Too The mystery becomes even deeper when we look at his name. The Sanskrit name Mārtāṇḍa has traditionally been connected with the idea of a “dead egg” or something associated with a lifeless egg. Different translations and interpretations of the ancient verse vary. That creates an extraordinary image. Aditi gives birth to eight sons. Seven become associated with the gods. But the eighth is connected with something that is dead, incomplete or lifeless. And yet... He is brought back. Why Did Aditi Bring Him Back? This may be the strangest part of the entire story. The next verse says that Aditi went forward with her seven sons, but brought Mārtāṇḍa back for procreation and death . Think about what that means. Mārtāṇḍa isn't simply rejected forever. He has a purpose. And that purpose is connected with the two things that define mortal existence: Birth. And death. This is why Mārtāṇḍa has remained such an intriguing figure for interpreters. Was Mārtāṇḍa the Sun? Here's where the story becomes complicated. A common later understanding connects Mārtāṇḍa with the Sun . Later Vedic and post-Vedic traditions use Mārtāṇḍa as a name or epithet associated with Sūrya , and traditional commentators also identify him with the Sun. There is also an interesting clue in the same Rigvedic hymn. The hymn describes the gods bringing forth Sūrya , who had been hidden in the ocean. So it is understandable why later tradition connected Mārtāṇḍa with the Sun. But there is a problem. The hymn itself never simply says: “Mārtāṇḍa is Sūrya.” That's why the story remains debated. Another Possibility: Mārtāṇḍa and Mortality The final verse gives us another clue. Mārtāṇḍa is brought back for birth and death. Because of this, some interpretations understand him not merely as a solar deity but as a figure connected with mortal existence itself — potentially even with the origin of mortal beings. This creates two very different ways of looking at him. One interpretation: Mārtāṇḍa → Sun → the cycle of rising and setting → birth and death. Another: Mārtāṇḍa → mortality → the beginning of the mortal order. Neither interpretation completely resolves the riddle. And that uncertainty is precisely what makes the story fascinating. The “Eight Sons” Are Not the Gods You Might Expect Another interesting detail is that the number of Ādityas changes across Vedic and later traditions. The Rigvedic hymn speaks of eight sons of Aditi. Later traditions develop different lists, and the classical Puranic tradition commonly speaks of twelve Ādityas . So the familiar idea that there has always been one fixed list of twelve Ādityas should not simply be projected backward onto this particular Rigvedic passage. The mythology was developing. The identities and relationships of these divine figures changed across different periods and texts. Mārtāṇḍa sits right inside that fascinating transition. So Was He Really a Forgotten Sun God? Maybe. But saying simply: “Mārtāṇḍa was the ancient name of Surya.” misses the strangest part of the story. The oldest text gives us something much more mysterious: Aditi gives birth to eight. Seven are taken to the gods. One is rejected. That one is Mārtāṇḍa. Then he is brought back. And his existence becomes connected with birth and death. Later traditions increasingly connect his name with the Sun. But the original hymn leaves us with an unanswered question: Why was the Sun — if Mārtāṇḍa was indeed the Sun — the one child Aditi cast away? The Sun That Dies Every Evening? There is a fascinating symbolic possibility here. The Sun appears every morning. It disappears every evening. It is born. It dies. And then it returns. If Mārtāṇḍa is understood as a solar figure, his connection with birth and death suddenly becomes remarkably appropriate. The Sun is the celestial body that seems to repeat this cycle every day. But we should be careful here. This is an interpretive reading , not something the Rigveda explicitly explains for us. The hymn gives us the mystery. Later traditions and interpreters give us different ways of understanding it. What Happened to Mārtāṇḍa? Perhaps the strangest answer is: He wasn't exactly forgotten. His name survived. His story survived. His association with the Sun survived. But the mysterious figure who appears in Rigveda 10.72 became increasingly absorbed into later understandings of Sūrya and the Ādityas . The strange eighth son gradually became less strange. And perhaps that's why we rarely hear his original story today. We remember Surya . We remember the Ādityas . But we don't often stop and ask: Who was the eighth son? The Forgotten Eighth Son Mārtāṇḍa is one of those figures who makes ancient mythology feel less like a collection of neatly finished stories and more like something that evolved over time. The oldest text doesn't hand us a complete biography. It gives us fragments. An ancient mother. Eight sons. Seven accepted. One rejected. A strange name. A return. And the mystery of birth and death. Perhaps Mārtāṇḍa was an early solar figure. Perhaps he represented mortality. Perhaps the ancient hymn deliberately allowed both ideas to exist. We don't know with certainty. And maybe that's the most interesting thing about him. Because sometimes the oldest stories don't answer our questions. They leave them behind. Beyond the Obvious Mārtāṇḍa is not simply a forgotten name for the Sun. He is a glimpse into a much older layer of Indian religious thought — a time when the identities of gods were not always as fixed and familiar as they became in later tradition. And somewhere inside that ancient hymn is an unanswered question: Why would Aditi cast away one of her own sons — only to bring him back for birth and death? We may never know exactly what the ancient poet intended. But the question has survived for thousands of years. And perhaps that is why Mārtāṇḍa deserves to be remembered. Sources & Notes The story of Mārtāṇḍa appears in Rigveda 10.72.7–9 . Translations differ, particularly in how Mārtāṇḍa's name and role are interpreted. Later traditions associate Mārtāṇḍa with the Sun, while interpretations of the original Rigvedic figure remain debated. © 2026 Beyond The Obvious · Sakshi Madgundi

But I Forgot One Important Thing. A website isn't really finished when it goes live. It's finished when the person who owns it can actually live with it. The mistake I made on my first client project. When I started working on my first client website, I had one very clear goal: make the existing application look and work like the client's website. The client already had a fully designed application. My task was to bring that experience into WordPress while keeping the same visual identity, layout and functionality. And I did it. The pages looked right. The interactions worked. The design matched the application. The website was live. But I didn't ask myself what would happen after I handed the website over. The part I didn't think about Build → Launch → ? I focused on making it work. Because the original application already existed, I concentrated heavily on reproducing what was already there. I worked on the custom UI, product pages, interactions, WooCommerce functionality and responsive behavior. I wanted precise control over the design. And that led me toward a lot of hard-coded implementation. My thinking at the time "If I can control the code, I can control the design." // Custom page structure // Custom styling // Custom interactions // Everything exactly where I want it And technically, that worked. But there was a problem hiding underneath that success. Hard-coded doesn't automatically mean maintainable. A hard-coded page can be functional. It can be fast. It can be beautifully designed. It can even give the developer extremely precise control. But then the client says: "I want to change this product image." Or: "I want to update the price." Or: "Can I change this text myself?" That's when the implementation starts to matter. The website should belong to the client. This is the part I understand much better now. When a developer creates a website for a business, they're not only delivering a collection of pages. They're delivering something the business will continue using after the developer leaves. A small change shouldn't require a developer Client wants to change price → Dashboard → Updated If changing a simple product price requires opening a PHP file, the client is dependent on the developer for something they should reasonably be able to manage themselves. The distinction I should have made earlier. There is an important difference between custom design and custom content management. You can build a highly customized website without making every piece of content permanently trapped inside the code. LAYER 01 · EXPERIENCE The custom website UI / UX Layout Custom CSS Interactions Animations Responsive behavior Complex functionality LAYER 02 · CONTENT The editable website Product names Prices Images Descriptions Promotional content Business information Blog content What the client should see. The developer can control the structure and experience, while the client gets a practical way to manage the content. PRODUCT EDITOR Save Changes Product name Product Name Here Price ₹950 Product image Change image → Description Edit description → Maintenance isn't an afterthought. This was probably the biggest lesson I took from that project. When someone says, "The website is complete," that doesn't necessarily mean the project is over. Websites live. Businesses change. Products change. Prices change. Plugins update. Browsers change. Customers request new features. And sometimes, something simply breaks. A website is not a poster. It's a living product. Website lifecycle 01 Design 02 Build 03 Launch 04 Maintain 05 Improve What does website maintenance actually mean? Maintenance isn't simply fixing a website when something breaks. ✦ Content Products, prices, images, banners, descriptions, contact information and new content. ⌘ Technical WordPress, themes, plugins, WooCommerce, PHP compatibility, JavaScript and integrations. ↗ UX Broken buttons, mobile issues, confusing navigation, outdated pages and inconsistent interfaces. ◈ Security Updates, backups, access permissions and keeping the website's software current. What I would do differently today. If I rebuilt that project today, I wouldn't start by asking: "How can I hard-code this page?" I'd start with a different question: The question I should have asked "Which parts of this page should the client be able to control?" Then I'd separate the website into the experience layer and the content layer. That doesn't mean everything needs to become editable. Some things should absolutely remain controlled by the developer. Complex JavaScript, layout systems, integrations, responsive behavior and technical functionality may need custom development. But content that changes regularly should have a sensible way for the client to manage it. A rule I'm taking forward If the client is expected to change it regularly, don't hide it inside the code. From "website developer" to "website partner." This changed how I think about web development. The job isn't simply: Design → Code → Deploy It's closer to: Understand → Build → Test → Launch → Maintain The lesson I learned from one project. I don't consider the hard-coded pages a completely wasted decision. They taught me something that tutorials couldn't: A developer doesn't only build for today's requirements. They build for the person who has to use the system tomorrow. And tomorrow, the client might want to change something. That's when maintainability stops being a technical detail and becomes part of the product. BEYOND THE OBVIOUS · DEVELOPER NOTES Remember Build it. Make it editable. Keep it healthy.
